words.definition: A person who habitually doubts or questions accepted beliefs and claims.
words.example: When the salesman promised the pills would cure everything, the skeptic demanded to see the research first.
words.mnemonic: A skeptic inSPECTs every claim before accepting it — same close-looking 'spect' as 'inspect'.

words.definition: Someone who believes people act only from self-interest and distrusts all good intentions.
words.example: The cynic assumed the billionaire's donation was just a tax dodge, not real generosity.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sick-nick' — he's sick of trusting anyone's motives.

words.definition: Too ready to believe things, often without demanding any proof.
words.example: So credulous was he that he wired money to a stranger claiming to be a lost prince.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'credo' = I believe; this person believes on command.

words.definition: Easily tricked or deceived because of being far too trusting.
words.example: The gullible tourist paid fifty dollars for a 'magic' rock the vendor had found on the beach.
words.mnemonic: To 'gull' means to fool; picture a gull bird swallowing anything tossed its way.

words.definition: Unwilling or unable to accept that something is true; showing open disbelief.
words.example: She gave an incredulous laugh when he claimed he'd run a marathon that morning.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' means not — someone who will NOT swallow what they hear.

words.definition: Acceptance that something is true or believable.
words.example: The eyewitness account lent credence to the theory that the fire was set deliberately.
words.mnemonic: Same 'cred' root as 'credit' — granting credence is extending mental credit.

words.definition: A firmly held belief or opinion.
words.example: She spoke with such conviction that the jury never doubted her sincerity.
words.mnemonic: To 'convince' shares the root — once convinced, you carry a conviction.

words.definition: Deeply committed to religion and its practices.
words.example: The devout grandmother attended mass every single morning before dawn.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'de-vow' — living entirely by one's sacred vows.

words.definition: Showing deep, sincere respect for religion and its duties.
words.example: The pious monk spent his days in prayer and quiet study.
words.mnemonic: 'Pi-' opens 'piety' — a person brimming with piety.

words.definition: Not connected with religious or spiritual matters.
words.example: They chose a secular ceremony at the town hall rather than a church wedding.
words.mnemonic: Think of the worldly, everyday realm kept separate from the sacred.

words.definition: An opinion that sharply conflicts with established religious beliefs.
words.example: Claiming the Earth circled the sun was once condemned as heresy by the Church.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'hairy-sea' — a wild, dangerous idea the orthodox fear to cross.

words.definition: A person who thinks it is impossible to know whether God exists.
words.example: Raised in no faith, she called herself an agnostic who simply couldn't be sure.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'a-' (not) + 'gnosis' (knowledge) — one who claims no knowing.

words.definition: Cautious or suspicious because of possible danger or trouble.
words.example: After being scammed once, he was leery of any deal that sounded too good.
words.mnemonic: Picture throwing a side-eye 'leer' at something you don't trust.

words.definition: A tendency to believe things too easily, without asking for proof.
words.example: The con artist preyed on the credulity of elderly investors desperate for quick returns.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'cred' (believe) with 'credit' — an overdraft of belief.

words.definition: Lacking experience, wisdom, or judgment; innocently trusting.
words.example: It was naive of him to think his first business would succeed without any planning.
words.mnemonic: From French for 'natural/native' — untouched by worldly experience.

words.definition: To formally give up or reject a claim, belief, or right.
words.example: After his conversion, he renounced all his worldly possessions and entered the monastery.
words.mnemonic: re + NOUNCE, like 'announce' — you publicly announce that you're giving something up.

words.definition: To take back a former statement or opinion, admitting it was wrong.
words.example: Under threat of execution, Galileo was forced to recant his claim that the earth moves.
words.mnemonic: re + CANT sounds like 'can't' — you now say you can't stand by what you said before.

words.definition: To take back or withdraw something said, offered, or extended.
words.example: The newspaper printed an apology and retracted the false story about the mayor.
words.mnemonic: re + TRACT (to pull, as in 'tractor') — you pull your words back in.

words.definition: To deny any connection with or responsibility for something.
words.example: The senator quickly disavowed the extremist group that had endorsed her campaign.
words.mnemonic: DIS (not) + AVOW (declare) — the exact opposite of owning it; you refuse to claim it.

words.definition: To check or prove that something is true or accurate.
words.example: The bank called to verify that I had actually made the large purchase.
words.mnemonic: VER- means truth in Latin (verus) — to verify is to make sure it's true.

words.definition: To state firmly and publicly that something is true.
words.example: She affirmed her loyalty to the team even after the crushing loss.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a FIRM' — you say it firmly and stand firm behind it.

words.definition: To admit or declare something openly and without shame.
words.example: He avowed his love for her in front of the entire wedding party.
words.mnemonic: a + VOW — like making a vow out loud for everyone to hear.

words.definition: To openly declare or claim something, sometimes falsely.
words.example: She professed to be an expert, though she had never studied the subject at all.
words.mnemonic: Think of a PROFESSor 'professing' knowledge aloud before a class.

words.definition: To claim or appear to be something, especially when the claim is doubtful.
words.example: The email purported to be from the bank, but it was actually a scam.
words.mnemonic: Like a fake PASSPORT that 'ports' itself as genuine — it claims to be what it isn't.

words.definition: To demand or specify a particular requirement as part of an agreement.
words.example: The contract stipulates that all work must be finished before the end of June.
words.mnemonic: A STIPulation is a strict point you must dot down in a deal — spell out the condition.

words.definition: To accept something as true without any proof.
words.example: I assumed the store was open, so I was surprised to find the door locked.
words.mnemonic: The old saying: to ASSUME can make trouble — because you took it for granted.

words.definition: To suppose something is true based on likelihood rather than proof.
words.example: Since no one answered the door, I presumed they had already left for work.
words.mnemonic: pre + SUME — you 'sum it up' beforehand, guessing from what seems probable.

words.definition: A statement or plan offered for others to consider or accept.
words.example: The investor listened carefully before rejecting the risky business proposition.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'propose' — a proposition is something set forth for consideration.

words.definition: A central idea or claim that an argument sets out to prove.
words.example: Her entire essay was built around the thesis that cities make people lonelier.
words.mnemonic: Greek for 'a setting down' — the position you set down and defend; its opposite is the anti-thesis.

words.definition: The quality of being accurate, honest, and in accordance with fact.
words.example: The detective questioned the veracity of the witness's shaky, shifting account.
words.mnemonic: VER- (truth, as in verify and verdict) + -acity — the state of being truthful.

words.definition: A false belief or flawed argument that seems logical but is mistaken.
words.example: The notion that money always brings happiness is a widespread fallacy.
words.mnemonic: FALL-acy — a belief where your logic FALLs apart.

words.definition: So weak, thin, or slight that it barely holds together.
words.example: After the scandal, his grip on power grew tenuous.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tenuis' (thin) — as thin as a single stretched thread.

words.definition: Able to make someone believe that something is true or right.
words.example: She gave such a convincing argument that everyone changed their minds.
words.mnemonic: CON + VINCE — Vince cons you until you believe him.

words.definition: Impossible to defend, justify, or maintain.
words.example: Once the new evidence surfaced, his position became untenable.
words.mnemonic: UN + TEN + ABLE — you're NOT able to hold (Latin 'tenere') your ground.

words.definition: Able to be justified, protected, or shown to be reasonable.
words.example: Her choice was defensible given the limited information she had.
words.mnemonic: DEFENSE + IBLE — something you can mount a DEFENSE for.

words.definition: So certainly true that no one can question or argue against it.
words.example: The DNA match was indisputable proof that he had been there.
words.mnemonic: IN + DISPUTE + ABLE — you are NOT able to DISPUTE it.

words.definition: Impossible to prove wrong or disprove.
words.example: The scientist presented irrefutable evidence for her theory.
words.mnemonic: IR + REFUTE + ABLE — no one is able to REFUTE it.

words.definition: Certain beyond any possibility of doubt or argument.
words.example: The photographs gave incontrovertible proof that the meeting took place.
words.mnemonic: IN + CONTROVERT — it stirs NO controversy; you can't turn against it.

words.definition: Clearly true and impossible to reject or dispute.
words.example: Her talent for singing is undeniable.
words.mnemonic: UN + DENY + ABLE — you are NOT able to DENY it.

words.definition: Not based on any fact, evidence, or good reason.
words.example: Their fears that the bridge would collapse proved unfounded.
words.mnemonic: UN + FOUNDED — it has no FOUNDATION to stand on.

words.definition: Having no support in fact, evidence, or reason.
words.example: The accusations were baseless and the court dismissed them quickly.
words.mnemonic: BASE + LESS — it has no BASE, nothing to rest on.

words.definition: To confirm or guarantee that someone or something is trustworthy.
words.example: I can vouch for her honesty; I've known her for years.
words.mnemonic: VOUCH sounds like VOW — you make a VOW that someone is good.

words.definition: To officially approve or permit an action or practice.
words.example: The committee voted to sanction the new research program.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with SANCTIFY — to give something official blessing.

words.definition: To accept or overlook wrong behavior without punishing it.
words.example: The school will not condone bullying of any kind.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'con-DONE' — you treat the wrong as done with and let it pass.

words.definition: To criticize or blame someone strongly and formally.
words.example: The senate voted to censure the official for misconduct.
words.mnemonic: CENSURE sounds like CENSOR — both deliver stern, public disapproval.

words.definition: To publicly condemn someone or something as wrong or evil.
words.example: At the rally, protesters gathered to denounce the corrupt mayor.
words.mnemonic: de- (down) + -nounce (announce): to announce someone DOWN, out loud and in public.

words.definition: To openly criticize something as bad or worthless.
words.example: Economists decry the new tariffs as harmful to small businesses.
words.mnemonic: de + CRY: you loudly CRY out against something you hate.

words.definition: Cruel mockery or teasing aimed at making someone look foolish.
words.example: She endured the ridicule of her peers after the flubbed speech.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ridiculous' — ridicule makes someone look ridiculous.

words.definition: A strong feeling that someone or something is worthless and deserves no respect.
words.example: She looked at the cheater with scorn and walked away.
words.mnemonic: SCORN sounds like SCORCH — you scorch someone with a burning, dismissive look.

words.definition: A strong feeling of disgust toward someone regarded as worthless or beneath respect.
words.example: He felt nothing but contempt for those who cheated to win.
words.mnemonic: 'Can't-tempt': they are so beneath you that they can't even tempt your attention.

words.definition: A feeling of superiority that makes someone regard others as unworthy.
words.example: She regarded the tabloid gossip with cool disdain.
words.mnemonic: dis + deign: you won't 'deign' to lower yourself — you 'dis' them as beneath you.

words.definition: A deep-seated feeling of dislike or hostility toward someone or something.
words.example: There was a long-standing antipathy between the two rival families.
words.mnemonic: anti- (against) + -pathy (feeling): a gut feeling AGAINST someone.

words.definition: An attitude of doubt about whether claims or beliefs are actually true.
words.example: Scientists greeted the miracle-cure study with deep skepticism.
words.mnemonic: A skeptic says 'SKIP it, I don't buy that' before believing anything.

words.definition: To destroy someone's mistaken but pleasant beliefs, leaving them let down.
words.example: The scandal disillusioned voters who had once trusted the party.
words.mnemonic: dis- + illusion: stripping away a comforting illusion someone was clinging to.

words.definition: A feeling of doubt or unease about a future outcome.
words.example: She signed the contract despite serious misgivings about the terms.
words.mnemonic: mis- (wrong) + giving: your gut is 'giving' you a wrong, uneasy signal.

words.definition: An uneasy feeling of doubt about whether an action is right.
words.example: He had no qualms about firing loyal employees to boost profits.
words.mnemonic: QUALM = 'calm' with a Q — the pang that disturbs your calm conscience.

words.definition: A nervous feeling of fear about something that may happen.
words.example: She approached the closed door with visible trepidation.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'trepidare' = to tremble — you tremble nervously before the big trial.

words.definition: Worry or anxiety that something bad is about to happen.
words.example: A wave of apprehension swept over her as the results loaded.
words.mnemonic: To 'apprehend' means to grasp — here fear grabs and holds onto you.

words.definition: Genuine and honest in feeling, without pretense or deceit.
words.example: Her sincere apology moved everyone in the room to forgiveness.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'sine cera' = 'without wax' — pure, with no cracks filled in to fake it.

words.definition: Open and honest in speech, even when the truth is unpleasant.
words.example: To be frank, your essay needs a complete rewrite before Monday.
words.mnemonic: Picture a guy named Frank who always says exactly what he thinks, bluntly.

words.definition: Deliberately vague or avoiding a direct answer so as not to be pinned down.
words.example: When reporters asked about the layoffs, the CEO gave evasive replies and quickly changed the subject.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'evade' — someone evasive keeps slipping away from your questions.

words.definition: Hard to find, catch, capture, or clearly understand.
words.example: The elusive snow leopard has been photographed only a handful of times in the wild.
words.mnemonic: E-LOOSE-ive: it stays loose and won't be caught.

words.definition: The act of deliberately misleading people while pretending to be honest.
words.example: Her duplicity became clear when we discovered she had been feeding secrets to our rivals all along.
words.mnemonic: 'Dupli-' means double (like duplicate) — a duplicitous person plays a double game.

words.definition: The act of hiding or twisting the truth in order to mislead someone.
words.example: The whole investment scheme was built on deceit, and thousands of families lost their savings.
words.mnemonic: Picture a con artist offering you a comfy 'seat' while quietly picking your pocket.

words.definition: The act of making someone believe something that is not true.
words.example: The magician's entire act relies on deception, guiding your eyes away from his hands.
words.mnemonic: De- + 'cept' (to take, as in capture) — deception takes your trust away.

words.definition: Clever, sneaky skill used to trick or outwit other people.
words.example: With sheer guile, the fox lured the guard dogs far away from the henhouse.
words.mnemonic: Hides inside be-GUILE — to beguile someone is to charm them with trickery.

words.definition: Clever at getting what you want through sly, sometimes dishonest tricks.
words.example: The cunning thief studied the guards' routines for weeks before making his move.
words.mnemonic: Think of the classic fox: quietly 'running' rings around every hunter.

words.definition: Full of clever tricks and good at fooling others to gain an edge.
words.example: The wily old negotiator let his opponent speak first, then twisted every word to his own advantage.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'wile' — Wile E. Coyote is forever scheming.

words.definition: Spreading harm gradually and secretly before the danger becomes obvious.
words.example: The disease is insidious, causing no symptoms until it has already damaged the organs.
words.mnemonic: 'Inside-ious' — the harm works quietly from the inside before you notice.

words.definition: Pretending to be sincere or honest while actually hiding your true motives.
words.example: It was disingenuous of him to claim total surprise when he had planned the whole thing.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (not) + 'genuine' — a disingenuous person is simply not genuine.

words.definition: Acting as if you are morally better than everyone else, in a smug, preachy way.
words.example: Spare me the sanctimonious lecture about honesty from a man who cheats on his taxes.
words.mnemonic: 'Sanct-' means holy (saint, sanctuary) — this is someone acting fake-holy.

words.definition: Claiming to hold moral standards that your own behavior clearly breaks.
words.example: There is a glaring hypocrisy in a climate minister who flies a private jet to every meeting.
words.mnemonic: From the Greek for a stage 'actor' — the hypocrite wears a mask: says one thing, does another.

words.definition: A false show put on to make people believe something that is not real.
words.example: Under the pretense of checking the meter, the stranger slipped quietly into the house.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pretend' — a pretense is a pretend act you put on for others.

words.definition: To teach a set of ideas repeatedly until someone accepts them without questioning.
words.example: The regime used its schools to indoctrinate children with loyalty to the party.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'doctrine' — to indoctrinate is to drill a doctrine into someone's head.

words.definition: To examine something very closely and carefully to find details or faults.
words.example: The auditors will scrutinize every receipt before approving the expense report.
words.mnemonic: 'Screw-tinize' — screw your eyes down tight to inspect every last detail.
